title: A Two-Stage Classifier with Reject Option for Text Categorisation
research_question: Can a text classifier improve overall classification reliability by rejecting uncertain category decisions at a first stage and automatically resolving those rejected decisions with a specialized second-stage classifier?
methodology: The study evaluates a two-stage reject-option architecture on the Reuters-21578 Mod-Apte text-categorization benchmark after retaining 7,769 training documents and 3,019 test documents over 90 categories. Documents are represented with TF-IDF bag-of-words features; the first stage uses either a multilayer perceptron or Naive Bayes, while rejected category assignments are passed to a modified category-specific k-nearest-neighbor second stage. Thresholds are tuned using validation data, and experiments vary first-stage rejection rates and the amount of data available to the second stage. Reported micro- and macro-averaged F1 values are averages over ten runs with randomly generated first-stage training subsets.

key_findings.finding: With an MLP first-stage classifier, the two-stage reject architecture raises micro-F1 from 0.846 to 0.854 and macro-F1 from 0.447 to 0.481 in the reported configurations.
With Naive Bayes at the first stage, reported micro-F1 rises from 0.700 to 0.825 and macro-F1 from 0.214 to 0.456 under the strongest shown reject configuration.
For a fixed first-stage reject rate, larger second-stage training sets generally produce larger improvements.
When the second-stage training and validation sets are too small, F1 can fall below the corresponding no-reject result.
In some configurations the tailored two-stage architecture outperforms a conventional k-NN classifier without rejection.
The whole two-stage system remains worse than the first-stage classifier evaluated only on decisions it accepted, because the second stage cannot correct every rejected assignment.

The reject-option concept is relevant as a general uncertainty-handling mechanism, but the study provides no direct evidence about event coreference, cross-thread identity, or enterprise email/chat continuity.

limitations: The authors describe the results as preliminary and evaluate only one benchmark dataset.
The method performs multi-label topical categorization, not event identity resolution or cross-document coreference.
The representation is based on TF-IDF bag-of-words features and classifiers characteristic of the period, limiting direct comparison with modern contextual models.
Performance depends on the amount of data available to the second stage, and undersized second-stage sets can make performance worse.
Automatic handling of rejects adds computational cost relative to a single-stage classifier.
No code release is identified in the accessible full text.
The paper does not evaluate temporal continuity, evolving event identity, cross-thread communication, or workplace-specific data.
raw_claims: The classifier may withhold category decisions that are considered insufficiently reliable.
Rejected category assignments are passed automatically to a second classifier so that no rejection remains in the final output.
The experiments use the Reuters-21578 Mod-Apte benchmark.
The processed data contain 7,769 training documents and 3,019 test documents across 90 categories.
Documents are represented using TF-IDF-weighted bag-of-words features.
The first-stage experiments use MLP and Naive Bayes classifiers.
The second stage uses a modified k-nearest-neighbor procedure specialized to rejected category decisions.
Thresholds are selected on validation data.
The reported F1 results are averaged over ten randomized runs.
The reject architecture improves MLP micro- and macro-F1 in the stronger configurations.
The reject architecture produces especially large absolute gains for the weak Naive Bayes baseline.
Larger second-stage training sets generally improve the treatment of rejected decisions.
A poorly provisioned second stage can reduce performance.
The final two-stage system cannot recover all errors that would theoretically be avoidable if rejected decisions were handled perfectly.
